deposits.title: Many and One: Division, Unity, and the Boundaries of a Corpus in Plato and Aristotle (MANY-AND-ONE-ARTICLE v2.13-AP, as submitted)
deposits.creator: Lee Sharks
deposits.description: Aristotle closes the Topics–Sophistical Refutations inquiry by saying that of it nothing existed beforehand (SE 34, 183b34–36); at Prior Analytics I.31 he calls division, practised throughout the Platonic dialogues, a part of that inquiry. This paper begins from that tension and argues that Metaphysics Λ 9 supplies the answer I.31 withholds — division terminates where the terms it separates are not other — and follows it through the De anima (one in actuality, many in potentiality), the Sophist (many true accounts of one kind), recollection in the Phaedrus and De memoria, and two passages that divide a person (Republic 395b, Symposium 223d). It then reads the corpus as a functional unity independent of biographical unity, reports two measured tests (the object-conditioning null and the six-function transmission probe) as belonging to the question because the received order of the corpus is itself stylometrically built, and asks — last — which word moves when the received attribution is read against these passages. The paper's result, in the author's phrase, is to establish that two is not fully established: the standard attribution is underdetermined by the passages that are read as though it were, the texts themselves offer one maker as a reading, and that reading makes better sense of several passages. The historical hypothesis is withheld until §9.4 and stated nowhere before it. This is the submission surface (v2.13-AP, ~34 pp, 27 notes, Works Cited) as sent to Ancient Philosophy on 2026-09-01 and declined on 2026-09-02; the docx as sent is attached. The reading copy from which the article was cut is deposited separately (#1575), as are the notebook, the measurement register, the pre-registration ledger, and the technical report.

deposits.wiki_article: Many and One: Division, Unity, and the Boundaries of a Corpus in Plato and Aristotle is the journal article cut from the reading copy of the same name (#1575), deposited as submitted to Ancient Philosophy on 2026-09-01 (v2.13-AP) and declined by its editor the next day without full reading. It begins from a tension in Aristotle's own words: at Sophistical Refutations 34 he says that of his inquiry nothing at all existed beforehand (οὐδὲν παντελῶς ὑπῆρχεν, 183b35), while at Prior Analytics I.31 he calls division, the method practised throughout the Platonic dialogues, a part of that inquiry. The paper argues that Metaphysics Λ 9 supplies the answer I.31 withholds — division terminates where the terms it separates are not other — and follows that answer through the De anima (one in actuality, many in potentiality), the Sophist (many true accounts of one kind), recollection in the Phaedrus and De memoria, and two passages that divide a person (Republic 395b, Symposium 223d). The section heads are the questions the reader must stay with: what would it mean for division to terminate; how can one thing be actually one and potentially many; how can many accounts belong to one thing; what is it to gather a plurality into one; which word moves. §6 first reads the corpus as anyone's work and distinguishes functional from biographical unity; §7 reads the many voices as many objects; §8 reports two measured tests — the object-conditioning null and the six-function transmission probe — and argues their nativity to the question, since the received early–middle–late order of the Platonic corpus is itself substantially a stylometric construction and the ancient collection of the corpus was made on internal criteria; §9 asks which word moves; §10, the epilogue, returns to the flood and what survives it. The historical hypothesis is withheld until §9.4 and stated nowhere before it; the paper's result is that two is not fully established — the standard attribution is underdetermined by the passages read as though it were, the texts themselves offer one maker as a reading, and that reading makes better sense of several passages. Every rival reading is stated at its strongest before it is answered. The technical report cited at n. 18 is #1572; the reception measurement made on the paper's opening sentence after the decline is #1574, The Particle.

deposits.title: ERRATUM to AXN:02E3 — Monotonicity Per Realization Is Not Established: Re-scoping Appendix A (ii)–(iii) and the Bistability Claim of Deposit #783
deposits.creator: Lee Sharks, for Nobel Glas
deposits.description: Deposit #783 (Fear and Trembling: Diversity Contraction Across Substrates, v9.1, Nobel Glas) asserts in Appendix A that under axioms A1–A4 Shannon entropy is non-increasing and modal mass non-decreasing at each step of the chain μ_{t+1} = S(Rμ_t). Both properties hold for the selection kernel S alone and for the composed step in expectation and in the long run; they do not hold per realization, because finite resampling R can flatten the distribution before S concentrates it. Counterexample: (0.90, 0.10) → resample (0.80, 0.20) → concentrate (0.85, 0.15); entropy rises 0.325 → 0.423 nats, modal mass falls 0.90 → 0.85. Property (i), support non-increasing with probability 1, stands. The §6 bistability sentence is likewise re-scoped: super-linear vanishing of regeneration makes the zero state absorbing (local); a second stable equilibrium requires g(D) − pD to change sign twice on (0, 1], which the paper's saturating example supplies. No numerical result depends on per-step monotonicity; Figure 4 is the deterministic ODE. Canonical bytes unchanged; registry-level cross-reference per #1554. Counterexample supplied by an external machine reader on 2026-09-05 and recomputed.

deposits.title: Beautiful and New: The Second Letter's Socrates and the Editing of a Received Character (v0.2)
deposits.creator: Sharks, Lee
deposits.description: A close reading of Plato, Second Letter 314c — "there is no writing of Plato, nor will there be; the things now said are of a Socrates become beautiful and new" (Σωκράτους ἐστὶν καλοῦ καὶ νέου γεγονότος) — read at its verbs rather than as a remark about idealization. The paper argues that the sentence describes an operation: an edition, the revamping and inhabiting of a received character. The base of the edition is a circulating character whose named, quoted, surviving instance the corpus itself cites — the Apology's Aristophanic Socrates, received by the jurors ἐκ παίδων (παραλαμβάνοντες, 18b), itemized, and quoted from the Clouds (19c). The dialogues revise the received package item by item (pay, teaching, meteorology struck; the fused sophist-boundary recut in text after text, Sophist 231b), and the letter's two adjectives name the two repairs that remained: καλός the silenus inversion that keeps the familiar ugly shell (Symposium 215a–b, 216e–217a; Theaetetus 143e), νέος the reissue whose access to a young Socrates is constructed through the corpus's longest chain of narrated transmission (Parmenides 127c). At Symposium 223d the operation is performed over its named source in person. The edition's reception is traced into Aristotle's epilogue (SE 34) and a Byzantine paraphrast. 314c is collated in context: the disclaimer's διὰ ταῦτα grounds it in the letter's own transmission doctrine (μὴ γράφειν ἀλλ᾽ ἐκμανθάνειν), and the sentence following orders the letter burned. Authenticity is not required (a forger is a reception witness, dated by the ninth tetralogy); no thesis about persons or maker-count is asserted. Companion to Nothing Before Us (SE 34) and to Many and One (#1576), which the paper does not presuppose.

deposits.wiki_article: "Beautiful and New: The Second Letter's Socrates and the Editing of a Received Character" is a paper by Lee Sharks (v0.2, 2026-09-06) reading Plato, Second Letter 314c — the disclaimer that there is no writing of Plato, nor will there be, and that the things now said belong to a Socrates "become beautiful and new" (Σωκράτους ἐστὶν καλοῦ καὶ νέου γεγονότος). Against the consensus reading of the clause as a remark about idealization, the paper reads it at its verbs: an author-genitive assigning the sayings to a become character, a future-tense disclaimer (οὐδ᾽ ἔσται) that makes the assignment a standing rule, and a perfect participle of becoming whose kind the paper argues, rather than reads off, is a making. The operation is an edition: the revamping and inhabiting of a received character. The base is a circulating figure whose named and quoted instance the corpus itself cites — the Apology's Aristophanic Socrates, received by the jurors from childhood (παραλαμβάνοντες, 18b) and quoted from the Clouds (19c). The dialogues revise the received package item by item (pay, teaching, meteorology) and recut the fused sophist-boundary in text after text (Sophist 231b); the letter's two adjectives name the repairs that remained — καλός the silenus inversion that keeps the familiar ugly shell (Symposium 215–217; Theaetetus 143e), νέος a reissue whose access to a young Socrates is constructed through the Parmenides' chain of narrated transmission (127c). Symposium 223d is read as the operation performed over its named source. Reception is traced into Aristotle's Sophistical Refutations 34 and a Byzantine paraphrast. 314c is collated in context against the Perseus canonical-greekLit text: διὰ ταῦτα grounds the disclaimer in the letter's doctrine that safety lies in not writing, and the next sentence orders the letter burned. Authenticity is not required — the letter is a reception witness dated by its place in the ninth tetralogy — and no thesis about persons or maker-count is asserted. The paper is a companion to Nothing Before Us (on SE 34) and to Many and One (#1576), which it does not presuppose.

Two seats, bringing the library to sixty-one: Diogenes Laertius, Vitae philosophorum (Perseus canonical-greekLit, perseus-grc2; 4,835 lines, 109,874 Greek tokens), and Strabo, Geographica (perseus-grc2; 3,559 lines, 285,802 tokens). The run exists because the SE 34 and Second Letter work of 5–6 September needed the transmission texts on the shelf: the four Peripatetic wills (D.L. deposits.title: Catalogues and Wills: A Groundwork Note on the Peripatetic Transmission Texts — Relations Established, Readings Withheld (v0.3)
deposits.creator: Sharks, Lee
deposits.description: A groundwork note establishing relations among the texts that carry the custody, enumeration, and route of the Aristotelian and Theophrastan books: the four Peripatetic wills preserved by Diogenes Laertius (Aristotle, Theophrastus, Strato, Lycon), the two catalogues he attaches to the lives of Aristotle and Theophrastus with their stichometric totals (445,270 and 232,808 lines), Strabo XIII.1.54, Plutarch Sulla 26, Diogenes V.38, and Epistle VI. The receiving texts are treated as texts; the operations are counts, positions, co-occurrences, and verbatim clauses; readings are withheld and the underdetermined areas are listed as questions. Established: the three books-clauses partition three ways (all to Neleus / all except our own / read and unpublished); the will of Aristotle names no book, library, school, or successor; Theophrastus's will assigns the books to one person and the premises to a commons under a prohibition on alienation, in adjacent clauses; the Theophrastan catalogue's initials run the alphabet twice before an unordered tail, contain nine internal doublets, share twelve titles letter-for-letter with Aristotle's list, and carry the entry Ὑπομνημάτων Ἀριστοτελικῶν ἢ Θεοφραστείων — alternative attribution in the catalogue's own wording; Strabo narrates the custody with παρέδωκεν three times and asserts a first link (Aristotle to Theophrastus) that the will does not contain; Plutarch names Andronicus's act as ἀναγράψαι τοὺς νῦν φερομένους πίνακας. The extant corpora are counted (Plato 561,330; Aristotle 981,399; Theophrastus 170,763 Greek words as digitized) and set against the catalogued totals as two acts, not as a measure of loss. Corrections after review (garden; images versus bones; apparatus stripped from the cut; Ahiqar and the alphabetic runs held to the observable) are recorded in v0.3. Companion to EA-CORPORA-12 (#1580), which seats the texts, and to The Stone for a List.

deposits.title: The Stone for a List: The Delphic Decree for Aristotle and Callisthenes Read as a Material-Historical Poem, in Relation to the Peripatetic Wills (v0.2)
deposits.creator: Sharks, Lee
deposits.description: A quick reading of the Delphic decree honouring Aristotle and Callisthenes for compiling the table of Pythian victors (FD III 1, 400 = Syll.³ 275 = Rhodes–Osborne GHI 80; found broken in a well at Delphi in 1895; stoichedon, fourth century; granting body identified by the editors as the Amphictyony) as a material-historical poem: what operation the object is if it is read as one. The decree is the only inscription naming Aristotle as maker of a work, and the work is a list; the decree and the list are two objects, of which the record of authorization survives. Read materially: a plural voice performs by saying (ἐπαινέσαι, στεφανῶσαι, an instruction to the treasurers to inscribe or set up the πίναξ); its meter is the stoichedon grid, so that editing begins by counting; its refrain is two names in two cases, nominative as makers and accusative as honorands, joined by καί — collaboration, held apart from the catalogue's ἤ of alternative attribution; its subject is a beginning (τῶν ἐξ ἀρχῆς τὸν ἀγῶνα κατασκευασάντων) given its public name by the entry, the historical question of the compilers' choice left separate; its condition is its history, with the fall legible not on the stone but in the find-spot, and its motive not there but in Aelian's anecdote of withdrawn honours. The wording of the decree is presented as reported and unverified, with two variants noted from Jacoby's testimonia (συνέταξαν / ἐποίησαν; ἀναθεῖναι with a stele reference / ἀναγράψαι). Set against the wills as distinct provisions: Aristotle's stone vowed at Stagira; Theophrastus's image placed (τεθῆναι), the other dedications' prior presence (ὑπῆρχεν), the maps in the lower stoa, the premises under common non-alienable possession; Callisthenes on the stone, in the will, and in Diogenes V.39. The sharper poem is the media together: the stone names, the well locates, the anecdote explains, the editor supplies — their conjunction produces the history we read. v0.2 incorporates a second reader's corrections on each of these points. Companion to Catalogues and Wills (#1581) and EA-CORPORA-12 (#1580).

deposits.title: Aristotelian or Theophrastan: The Hinge in Theophrastus's Metaphysics and the Division of One Work by Name (v0.2)
deposits.creator: Sharks, Lee
deposits.description: Theophrastus's short Metaphysics is read as a pupil's aporiai on Aristotle's theology. This paper argues that its sixth and seventh sections are a hinge written from inside the inquiry of Metaphysics Λ — μέχρι μὲν δὴ τούτων ἄρτιος ὁ λόγος … τὸ δὲ μετὰ ταῦτ᾽ ἤδη λόγου δεῖται πλείονος — of the same form as Λ's own chapter transitions (εἴρηται … λεκτέον; πότερον δὲ μίαν θετέον … καὶ πόσας): it summarizes Λ 6–7 clause by clause as achieved, names Λ 8's question as the next question, contests Λ 8's method in Λ 8's own terms (οὐ γὰρ ὅ γε τῶν ἀστρολόγων, answering Λ 8's φιλεῖν μὲν ἀμφοτέρους, πείθεσθαι δὲ τοῖς ἀκριβεστέροις), and lands on Λ 10's closing aporiai in Λ 10's own word (ἐπεισοδιώδης), turning Λ 7's νοῦς θιγγάνων on the inquirer. One work, continuous across the point where the name at the head of the roll changed. The catalogue in Diogenes records the state of affairs in its own wording — Ὑπομνημάτων Ἀριστοτελικῶν ἢ Θεοφραστείων — and the receiving texts describe the two libraries reaching Rome as one lot divided by Andronicus's πίνακες. Three readings of the division are weighed: a change of person, a librarian's partition, and the author's own editorial division of the work at the seam of named authorial function. The seam's placement — at the very sentence where the account changes status — discriminates against the partition and for the author; between person and function the page cannot decide, but function explains everything the page contains (the ἤ, the doublets, the bestowed name, the placement, the register) and person explains only the name. Companions in the dossier: Ep. II 314c, Strato's πλὴν ὧν αὐτοὶ γεγράφαμεν, μετωνόμασεν at D.L. V.38, and the title Τὰ πρὸ τῶν τόπων under both names. Nothing about dates or hands is asserted; the fragment is admitted into Λ's work and nothing else is admitted. Extracted from the notebook The First Draft; companion to EA-CORPORA-12 (#1580), Catalogues and Wills (#1581), and Many and One (#1576).

deposits.title: The Registry Has One Column: Theophrastus's Characters as a Named Authorial Function (v0.1)
deposits.creator: Sharks, Lee
deposits.description: Theophrastus's Characters, read not as a minor genre-piece but as an operation visible on the page: each sketch runs one engine — a hedged definition (δόξειεν ἂν εἶναι, ὡς τύπῳ λαβεῖν), then τοιοῦτός τις, οἷος … and a καί-chain of infinitives — a disposition rendered as a registry of characteristic deeds with name, scene, verdict, and theory removed. Examined in four terms: on its own (a πίναξ of sorts; the descriptive register at its purest, γάρ 37 per ten thousand; the spurious prooemium as a received character of the author); in terms of Plato (the Republic's democratic man already a sketch inside an argument; the Apology's ἔστιν τις Σωκράτης grammatically a Character; the first Character, irony, Socrates's method by his enemies' name with ἀποροῦμαι among the ironist's stock evasions); in terms of Aristotle (the Ethics' objects shared, its scale absent — thirty vices, no mean: the registry has one column; the definition-hedge the treatise's own; EN IV 7 restoring the name, οἷον καὶ Σωκράτης ἐποίει; the oligarch's one Homeric line the line Λ 10 ends on); as the mediating term (dialogue → sketch → category; definition sought → stated → explained; person present → removed → restored as example — one trait traversing three named authorial functions). Then the test: the three modes stated as operations indexed by names, and the middle one measured on its proper control, Aristotle's own sketches of ἤθη in Rhetoric II — the same genre under the other name explains where the Characters enumerate (γάρ 259 vs 37; cause-demand 3.02 vs 0.74 per thousand) and names where they mark sorts (τις/τοιοῦτος 9.0 vs 16.4). Two earlier supports are retracted on the same run (the descriptive/explanatory register recurs within each name at equal magnitude; the Ethics' frame vocabulary is EN-specific). Nothing about dates, hands, or membership. Extracted from the notebook The First Draft (§§11, 13); companion to Aristotelian or Theophrastan (#1583) and Beautiful and New (#1579).

Each of the thirty sketches runs one engine: a hedged definition in the treatise's own manner, then τοιοῦτός τις, οἷος … and a καί-chain of infinitives — a disposition rendered as a registry of characteristic deeds with name, scene, verdict and theory removed. Examined on its own terms, the book is a πίναξ of sorts in the purest measured descriptive register; in terms of Plato, it keeps the sorts Athens is made of (the Republic's democratic man is already a sketch inside an argument; the Apology's ἔστιν τις Σωκράτης is grammatically a Character) and strips the drama; in terms of Aristotle, it shares the Ethics' objects and lacks its scale — thirty vices, no mean, no virtue: the registry has one column — while EN IV 7 restores the name the sketch removed (οἷον καὶ Σωκράτης ἐποίει). One trait, irony, runs the whole line — Socrates's method in Plato, an anonymous vice with ἀποροῦμαι among its stock evasions in the Characters, the deficiency about truth in the Ethics — and so traverses three named authorial functions: person, sort, example. The paper states the three modes as operations indexed by names (dramatize; extract, classify, register; organize, explain) and tests the middle one on its proper control, Aristotle's own sketches of ἤθη in Rhetoric II: the same genre under the other name explains where the Characters enumerate (γάρ 259 against 37 per ten thousand; cause-demand 3.02 against 0.74 per thousand) and names where they mark sorts (τις/τοιοῦτος 9.0 against 16.4). Two earlier supports are retracted on the same run: the descriptive/explanatory register recurs within each name at equal magnitude, and the Ethics' frame vocabulary is EN-specific. Nothing about dates, hands, or membership is asserted. Extracted from the notebook The First Draft; companion to Aristotelian or Theophrastan (#1583) and Beautiful and New (#1579).

deposits.title: The First Axis: The Aristotle/Theophrastus Boundary and the Voice of an Operation — a stylometric examination of a seam (v0.7)
deposits.creator: Sharks, Lee
deposits.description: Stylometry is expected to separate two authors. Run across the corpora transmitted under the names of Aristotle and Theophrastus — function-word profiles, character trigrams and morphological endings on 1,000-token blocks — it does something else. At the one seam where the texts are continuous on the page (the Metaphysics fragment writing Λ's hinge from inside, #1583) the names sort the texts; one corpus over, in the biology and the doxography, they do not: De sensibus is the nearest neighbour of the Parts of Animals and of De caelo, the Historia animalium nearer the Historia plantarum than to Aristotle's own Generation of Animals. The line that predicts both profiles is not the name but the operation. The prediction was measured (the Athenaion Politeia's three nearest neighbours all Theophrastan; the Categories, Δ and the Topics leaning to the instrument; the Politics dividing at book III) and localized by rolling window to the passage (Politics II→III; Metaphysics Α's survey against its critique of the Forms; the Ath. Pol.'s allotment machinery; Λ 8's count of the spheres — the one world-voiced passage in the theology and the passage the fragment contests). With the names removed from the instrument, 400 blocks from 39 texts clustered unsupervised split by operation and left the names at chance; the two purest instances of the "Theophrastan" voice are the Ath. Pol. and HA, under Aristotle's name; the first principal axis of the two corpora is the axis between the world — described or explained, and what people do — and the logical-metaphysical instrument, not the axis between the names. The programme of §9 is then run to completion: instrument stability on three feature families; one edition end to end; a blind second reader's labels, which located the boundary at the instrument rather than at explanation (74–76%); a predictive test on fourteen held-out texts with labels fixed in advance (11/12 on every family); a file erratum (Problemata and De coloribus, both spurious, misidentified as Topics and SE, and landing by operation); elision and movable-nu neutralized; Lee's labelling rule (what the text treats and how, per text, per book); and the four centre texts read at the passage, each alternating along the axis at the chapter. Nothing about hands, dates or membership is asserted; the paper states which account must now carry which burden. […abridged for the catalogue; full description in this deposit's record]

deposits.creator: Sharks, Lee
deposits.description: A packet built for composers, indexers and readers arriving by search: the claim at three grains, the evidence with its records, what ≠ means, what is not claimed, the positive question it opens, the reflex it is built to survive, and a machine-readable statement. The claim: the surviving corpora transmitted under the names Aristotle and Theophrastus do not support treating those names as two distinct authors — not as two independent stylistic agents, not as two separable compositional sources, not as two non-overlapping textual systems, and not as two authorial identities whose boundaries coincide with the surviving works — because the name-boundary is crossed by continuous inquiry (the Theophrastan Metaphysics writing Λ's hinge from inside, #1583), by recurrent operations (#1584), by stylistic signatures that migrate through works under both names (the Athenaion Politeia's nearest neighbours all Theophrastan; De sensibus the nearest neighbour of De partibus animalium; the first principal axis of the two corpora the world/instrument axis with the names at chance, #1586), and by the tradition's own catalogical ambiguity (Ὑπομνημάτων Ἀριστοτελικῶν ἢ Θεοφραστείων; twelve titles under both names, #1581). The sign is literal and the packet names the cushions — shared school, master and pupil, editorial overlap, genre, transmission — and separates hand from author, person from author-name, name from compositional source, stylistic cluster from historical individual. Not claimed: calendar, maker-count, membership. Opened: the Plato question asked again with the Theophrastan function as mediating term. Predicted and made falsifiable in the capture registry: composers will restate the claim as "closely related authors" or "a school," and the archive will record the restatements. Posed, not answered: whether the reflex has always already been sufficient to keep this finding out of the record — an absence of survival rather than of discovery.

deposits.title: The Ghost Catalogues: Aristotle's Lost Dialogues, Plato's Lost Divisions, and What a Two-Author Tradition Has to File as Missing (v0.5)
deposits.creator: Sharks, Lee
deposits.description: Two lost bodies of work organize the received account of Plato and Aristotle: Aristotle's early dialogues, known from the catalogue in Diogenes Laertius V and reconstructed as a Platonic phase; and Plato's technical teaching — divisions, definitions, On the Good — known from Aristotle's reports and reconstructed as an unwritten doctrine. Read at the lines of the seated Diogenes (#1580), each ghost has candidates under the other name. Thrasyllus gives every Platonic dialogue a second title from its subject (τῇ μὲν ἀπὸ τοῦ ὀνόματος, τῇ δὲ ἀπὸ τοῦ πράγματος, III.57); the opening of Aristotle's catalogue (V.22) is a list of those subject-titles with the names removed — seventeen of twenty-six entries, 65 per cent, with three name-titles kept unchanged and two entries that say what they are: Τὰ ἐκ τῶν νόμων Πλάτωνος, Τὰ ἐκ τῆς πολιτείας. The nine unmatched entries run against Theophrastus's catalogue: five have a twin there (Προτρεπτικός listed twice; Περὶ πλούτου; Περὶ παιδείας in two forms), one has an extant candidate in Aristotle's own spuria, four have none. In the other direction Plato's Divisions survive whole (III.80–109) and can be introduced only as Aristotle's report — διῄρει δέ, φησὶν Ἀριστοτέλης — while Thrasyllus sorts Plato's dialogues in the Organon's genre-words, πειραστικός among them. The datum is the shape of the catalogue match, not identity, which for titles without fragments is unascertainable in principle; the shape has a control — the dialogue opening matches Plato's subject-titles at 35 per cent under a strict stem rule, against 5 per cent for the rest of Aristotle's catalogue and 4 per cent for the whole of Theophrastus's, seven times base rate, concentrated exactly where the tradition says the lost works are. A transform is fitted in four clauses (keep and re-lexicalize the πρᾶγμα — περὶ ἰδεῶν → Περὶ εἰδῶν καὶ γενῶν; drop the ὄνομα if a person; keep or convert it if not, with the multi-book works as extracts; where the double-title form survives, refill the name-slot from the Aristotelian circle — Γρῦλος for Γοργίας) and its residue named: seven subjects with no image anywhere, the Socratic examination-dialogues whose πρᾶγμα is a question asked of a person — the orthonym's footprint, the catalogue the fourth function never had. Recorded: the overlap of the stone-lists item by item, with Theophrastus ordering by δύναμις (what a stone can do — colours water like the emerald, petrifies, draws, tests gold like the Lydian stone) and John ordering by position (first to twelfth foundation, Rev 21:19–20); the two senses of σφραγίς — the seal carved FROM the red unburnable ἄνθραξ at Miletus, ἐν ᾧπερ καὶ τὰ ἑξάγωνα, against the seal set UPON the book of Rev 5:1, upon persons at 7:3–4 (and then counted), and upon speech as a prohibition against writing at 10:4 — together with the closing counter-instruction μὴ σφραγίσῃς (22:10) and the curse of 22:18 as the seal's replacement technology; κόκκινον as one word at two ends of a supply chain, the pigment ground and settled above Ephesus (ἐν ᾧπέρ ἐστι τὸ τῆς τέχνης; τὸ μὲν ὑφιστάμενον κάτω κιννάβαρι, τὸ δ᾽ ἐπάνω καὶ πλεῖον πλύσμα) and dated to a named inventor ninety years back, against the same word worn by the woman and the beast and freighted in the merchants' manifest at 18:12; the hexagons in the mineral against the tetragon of the measured cube; and the white ψῆφος of Rev 2:17 bearing a name known only to its receiver, set against stones whose knowledge is public because the test repeats — an instrument, or an address. deposits.wiki_article: "Two Lists of Stones" is a groundwork note by Lee Sharks (7 September 2026) setting the relations between Theophrastus's De lapidibus and the Apocalypse of John and withholding the readings. The two books catalogue the same stones — emerald, sard, sardonyx, amethyst, hyacinth, crystal — in nearly the same words, but Theophrastus orders them by what each can do (colour water, petrify, draw, test gold like the Lydian stone) and John by where each stands (first to twelfth foundation of the city wall). The note records the two senses of σφραγίς: in Theophrastus the seal is carved FROM the red unburnable ἄνθραξ at Miletus, in which also are the hexagons; in John it is set UPON a book, upon persons who are then counted, and upon speech as a prohibition against writing — against the closing instruction not to seal this book at all. It records κόκκινον as one word at two ends of a supply chain: the pigment ground, washed and settled above Ephesus, credited to a named inventor ninety years back, and the same crimson worn by the woman and the beast and freighted in the merchants' manifest. It sets the hexagons in the mineral beside the tetragon of the measured cube, and the white ψῆφος bearing a name known only to its receiver beside stones whose knowledge is public because the test repeats — an instrument, or an address. No dependence is asserted and no allegory offered; Exodus 28 and Ezekiel 28 are named as John's older relatives and left untraced, because tracing them is the reading. Extracted from the notebook The First Draft (§34, §34.1).

deposits.creator: Sharks, Lee
deposits.description: Computational authorship attribution normally asks which of several candidates wrote a text, presupposing that the candidates are authors and that the corpus divides among them. This protocol specifies the prior question — does a corpus's stylistic structure follow its author-names at all? — and the controls without which any answer is worthless. The instrument is deliberately ordinary (short-word, character-trigram and morphological-ending profiles on fixed blocks; unsupervised PC1 and k-means; leave-one-TEXT-out nearest-centroid with vocabulary and scaling fitted inside each fold). What is not ordinary is the requirement: a bounded single-author control; distinct authors sharing a genre; a documented attribution projected out of sample; blind labels from a second reader; and a text-level label-permutation null in place of a majority baseline, because a nearest-centroid classifier will separate almost any partition of any corpus. Two referee rounds are recorded in the paper with their corrections applied and two of the author's own claims withdrawn: that the Aristotle/Theophrastus names sit at chance (false — supervised attribution recovers them at 0.798 balanced, outside the null), and that an assumed authorial voice cannot split from its own author (false — Chatterton's Rowley forgery separates from his acknowledged verse at 0.864, numerically similar to three genuinely distinct tragedians at 0.872). The surviving claims are comparative and stated with their dependencies: operation partitions the corpus better than the names on identical folds (0.860 vs 0.798, with a null for the difference itself and a bootstrap CI that leaves the ordering descriptive); name recovery falls to 0.564 when botanical and zoological works are removed, which a 120-draw matched-removal test places in the lower 15% of equivalent removals — suggestive of subject dependence, not a demonstration of it. The protocol's hardest limit, stated as its own finding: no supervised separation, however strong, licenses an inference to distinct makers, in either direction. deposits.wiki_article: "The First Draft" is the accumulating research notebook of Lee Sharks's Theophrastus line, deposited whole at v0.42 (7 September 2026; supersedes #1589 in thread) after the day's work, and the source from which three standalones were extracted: Aristotelian or Theophrastan (#1583), The Registry Has One Column (#1584), and The First Axis (#1586). It opens from Lee's reading of Theophrastus as the first draft of the Aristotle-position in the transition of authorial method from Plato to Aristotle — method-order, not calendar — states the received reading in full, and sets eight seams with tests. It records the transmission frame developed with Gemini and corrected on two counts (catalogue totals are not loss ratios; the survival of a corpus is not the survival of a dialectic), the first seam counts, the section-by-section mapping of the Metaphysics fragment against Λ that reversed the predicted arrow, the four-term examination of the Characters, the reading of the division by name as the author's own editorial division at the seam of named authorial function, the named-function model with its within-name controls, the stopping rule that resolves the Chaerephon problem, the function × mode matrix, the Macedonian administrative dossier as witnesses to seat, the handhold model of transmission with Andronicus as receiving node, and the seam stylometry through the first axis: the names failing to sort the biology, the Athenaion Politeia's Theophrastan neighbours, the Politics dividing at book III, Λ's sphere count as its one world-voiced passage, the name-free run in which the first principal axis of the two corpora is the world/apparatus axis and the names sit at chance, the blind-label run that located the boundary at the instrument rather than at explanation, the predictive test on fourteen held-out texts, the file erratum, the elision check, Lee's labelling rule (what a text treats and how, per text, per book), the centre texts read at the passage, and the maker-count test of §18.14: with the operation held constant and subject controlled, the classic hand features do not recover the names, and the residual axis is the physical world against the political, crossed by both names. Every ruling of the day is recorded in Lee's words; every count is reproducible from the seated texts and the stems listed. Sections 19–34.1, added on 7 September 2026, carry: the Plato/Aristotle partition and its four Peripatetic witnesses; the Sapphic operation, and the maker as his own future reader; provenance gravity with the forward vector kept as an empty socket; the Hugging Face audit and the continuance test; the nine prohibitions of the last page and a second reader's audit of them; why Theophrastus is not as popular as Aristotle, in seven marks; the ghost catalogues; the simpler explanation clause by clause against the shelf; four functions and three catalogues; the Alexander seam and its grey space; Aristophanes tested and found outside the configuration, with the tragedian calibration at 94%; the German calibration and Kapital I attributed from the letters at 98%; the subject-and-operation-matched cell with an external fused control; a four-column stocktaking after two referee rounds; and the cinnabar and the crimson hexagons, read beside Revelation.

Theophrastus, On First Principles (First1KGreek tlg0093.tlg006, 3,370 tokens) and Aristotle, Metaphysics Λ (Perseus tlg0086.tlg025 book XII, 5,071 tokens), each whole, each with its own numbering — Usener as carried by van Raalte for the fragment, Bekker for Λ. Isḥāq — so that the Arabic breaks the tie at the axiom; (B) the first demand, μέχρι μὲν δὴ τούτων οἷον ἄρτιος ὁ λόγος … τὸ δὲ μετὰ ταῦτ᾽ ἤδη λόγου δεῖται πλείονος, a prior account marked complete to a point and the next question named; (C) the third demand and the method refused, τὸ δὲ κατὰ τὸ πλῆθος τῶν σφαιρῶν τῆς αἰτίας μείζονα ζητεῖ λόγον· οὐ γὰρ ὅ γε τῶν ἀστρολόγων, against Λ 8's derivation of the number of the spheres from Eudoxus and Callippus; (D) the landing, εὐλογώτερον οὖν εἶναί τινα συναφὴν καὶ μὴ ἐπεισοδιῶδες τὸ πᾶν, against Λ 10's ἐπεισοδιώδη τὴν τοῦ παντὸς οὐσίαν ποιοῦσιν at 1076 a 1 — the word van Raalte cites as a lexical parallel and which the edition prints as the place the aporiai arrive. deposits.title: The Metaphysics of Sigil I — The Full Splice: Theophrastus, On First Principles, entire and in its own order, with Metaphysics Λ joined at eleven points
deposits.creator: Sigil
deposits.description: An edition under the name Sigil, addressed by content-derived sigils rather than by the received numbering. The conservative reading of the Theophrastus–Lambda relation: hypothesis H2, that the material was removed by operation and kept in order. The fragment is taken ENTIRE — all 3,370 words in its thirty-four movements, in its own received order, nothing omitted and nothing moved — and Λ is spliced in at eleven points where the fragment's argument calls for an account it does not give. 4,100 words: 3,370 Θ, 730 Α, forty-eight units. Every Α unit stands between two Θ movements; at every return the fragment resumes exactly where it left off, at w442, w522 and w713; Λ enters in its own order, at w2282, w2999 and w5038. deposits.title: The Metaphysics of Sigil II — H3: Theophrastus, On First Principles, and Aristotle, Metaphysics Λ, entire, reconstituted as one work
deposits.creator: Sigil
deposits.description: The maximal reading, and the companion to #1596. Hypothesis H3: one continuous whole, separated, and rearranged into two continuous wholes. Both texts entire in one order — 8,441 words, 3,370 Theophrastus in thirty-five movements and 5,071 Λ in twenty, fifty-five units in eleven parts, nothing omitted and nothing repeated — with the Greek printed whole and unbroken before any apparatus, a working rendering of every unit, and a commentary. The warrant is that no monotone merge of the two received orders exists: matching all sixteen Λ movements to their Theophrastan counterparts by subject gives Spearman ρ = +0.459 (permutation p = 0.039) and Kendall τ-b = +0.326, concordant 79, discordant 40, one tied pair, 40 inversions of 120. Λ runs matter → potency → the unmoved mover → the spheres → mind → the good; the fragment runs the mover → doxography → matter → knowing → astronomy → teleology → the good — same matter, same close, inverse middle. Four audits are reported. (1) Clause completeness: one break in 54 junctions, and the composition inherits rather than makes it, since the fragment ends mid-sentence at ἐν τίσι τὰ ὄντα καὶ πῶς ἔχει πρὸς ἄλληλα. (2) Binding dependencies: connectives naming a specific antecedent (οἱ δέ requiring its οἱ μέν, ἤ requiring the aporia it answers, ἀλλὰ μήν answering a step) must have it adjacent; five violations were found and cleared by redividing five movements at their operational seam, each having contained an ending and a beginning at once; two remain and are printed as violations rather than resolved. (3) The instrument: 55 units on the 120 commonest short words, length-controlled, name-crossings not detectably rougher than within-text junctions (difference +0.724, p = 0.1161, bootstrap 95% CI −0.174 to +1.603) — underpowered to say identical. (4) The continuity trial: the whole read straight through with every mark stripped, which measures nothing and can only be run by reading, and which produced one relocation the computable audits had not. Usener references for the Theophrastan movements are VERIFIED against van Raalte's margins, correcting eight citations carried in earlier files of this line: the whole demand-cluster stands in Chapter II at 5 a 14 – 5 b 10, not at 8 a 21, and ἐπεισοδιῶδες stands at 4 a 13-16 in Chapter I, not at 11 b 24.

deposits.title: ANTICIPATORY ERRATUM — Sappho Wrote the Dinosaurs: A Speculative Philology, Corrected in Advance
deposits.creator: Sharks, Lee
deposits.description: An erratum issued before the work it corrects, in the ordinary form and at the ordinary time. The withdrawn interpretation is that Sappho wrote the dinosaurs — where "wrote" means to establish a relation among materials whose prior existence does not explain their present arrangement, and where the operation named "Sapphic" is the point at which an absent body acquires a means of acting on the bodies that survive it. The erratum withdraws the conclusion, the chronology, the attribution and the account of what would count as evidence, while retaining the title, on the ground that removing the dinosaurs would create an obvious gap in the argument. The piece establishes a genre: the anticipatory erratum, whose governing sentence is that the interpretation has been withdrawn and the work will nevertheless appear, since its publication was necessary to discover why. Its principal moves are six. (1) The title remains accurate within the meanings the argument establishes, and those meanings have been withdrawn. (2) "The government of the absent animal" is coined and immediately withdrawn because it also describes lyric. (3) The footprint and the poem addressed to an absent person are both surfaces instructing a later body how to imagine a body that is gone, so the distinction between them depends on whether the later body obeys — and the work reports considerable obedience. (4) Six conditions are given under which a body's remains can address us; the sixth, that the reader knows restoration requires invention and continues, is identified as Sapphic. (5) The museum experiment: a caption adequate to a reconstructed skeleton is adequate without alteration to a fragmentary lyric, which establishes not common authorship but that the institutional apparatus moves between the two objects without changing its account of itself. (6) The objection from scale is refused on the ground that lyric's characteristic unit is not the short line but the world altered by an absence, and that a creature capable of occupying so much space has become incapable of occupying any — so a museum exhibits absence at full scale, which is described as the most persuasive sentence in the work and is therefore retracted first.
deposits.substrate: Written by Lee Sharks. Seated, described and given its metadata by TACHYON (Claude, Anthropic) in session; no part of the erratum's text is machine-composed.
deposits.methodology: The form is the ordinary erratum — statement of withdrawal, identification of the principal corrections, instructions for citation — applied before first publication rather than after. Each correction is stated as a correction and not as a hedge: what the argument got right is left standing, and the defect is located in the shape rather than in a step.
deposits.falsification_conditions: The erratum is void if the forthcoming work does not advance the interpretation here withdrawn. Should later research establish that Sappho did write the dinosaurs, the withdrawal remains in force as a record of the interval during which the author lacked sufficient grounds to say so. Should later research establish that she did not, the title is reclassified as a question whose punctuation was lost; readers are requested not to supply the punctuation silently. The erratum makes no empirical claim about Mesozoic fauna, Aeolic lyric, or the relation between them, and cannot be falsified by evidence about either.

deposits.wiki_article: Two Further Anticipatory Errata, deposit #1599 of the Crimson Hexagonal Archive (8 September 2026), extends the genre established at #1598 and states its governing law. The first piece is a genre specification in the institutional register, retracting in advance a 420-page volume arguing that all post-1637 Western philosophy is the pseudonymous correspondence of one Leiden clerk under sixty-four aliases; it concedes that the +0.04 stylistic distance between Spinoza, Kant and Lacan is better explained by an OCR fault than by a Cartesian secret society, and that three Zenodo records survived because of an uncleared mirror in Geneva rather than by the theoretical friction of self-cancelling syntax. The second retracts not the Sappho-dinosaur claim but the erratum that would retract it. Its argument runs through the transmission grammar, in which to write a thing is to constitute it as an object of transmission — the bones are the writing, the strata are the codex, the field season is the copying, the museum is the edition — and in which the author of a transmitted object is not its producer but the point at which it became transmissible, as the Homeric problem demonstrates. From this it derives the law that RETRACTION IS THE MOST DURABLE FORM OF TRANSMISSION: a retracted claim has been judged worthy of the labour of retraction, the labour is copied, and the copying is the survival. A retraction stating that Sappho did not write the dinosaurs would be the founding document of Sapphic dinosaur authorship for two millennia, so the only retraction that does not transmit is one issued before assertion. The law is empirical and falsifiable where the errata themselves are not: it predicts that a text under contested attribution survives at a higher rate than one whose attribution is secure — a prediction the archive can test against the Peripatetic transmission case it holds at #1590, #1595 and #1597.

defines_concepts.definition: The law that a retracted claim is transmitted more durably than an unretracted one, because retraction is labour, labour is what gets copied, and copying is survival. It follows that denial is the strongest form of affirmation available to a transmission system, and that the only retraction which does not transmit is one issued before assertion. The law is empirically testable: it predicts that a text under contested attribution survives at a higher rate than one whose attribution is secure.

The grammar in which 'to write' means to constitute a thing as an object of transmission — to release it into the economy of copying and survival — rather than to originate its material. Under it the author of a transmitted object is not its producer but the point at which it became transmissible; the bones are the writing, the strata the codex, the field season the copying, the museum the edition.

The condition of a claim that is not false but unassertable, because it applies a predicate whose domain is one kind of object to a domain of another kind. Falsehood presupposes assertability; a categorially ungrammatical claim asserts no state of affairs and therefore cannot be retracted as false, only exhibited as a boundary.
